hook: Why do you eat dessert when you are already full, practice an instrument nobody pays you to play, and freeze on a test you studied hard for? Motivation is whatever starts, directs and keeps behavior going, and psychologists have several theories, each good at explaining a different kind of "why".

prereq.q: Which brain structure helps keep the body's internal balance, including hunger and thirst?
prereq.why: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature and other parts of homeostasis.

prereq.q: A child gets a sticker every time she cleans her room, and she cleans more often. Which concept explains the increase?
prereq.why: Adding something pleasant after a behavior makes it more likely: positive reinforcement.

figure.caption: Performance is best at a moderate level of arousal; harder tasks peak at lower arousal.

chain.cause: The body lacks something it needs, such as water
chain.effect: a drive (thirst) pushes you to act, and drinking restores homeostasis: drive-reduction theory

chain.cause: An attractive reward is in view, such as dessert
chain.effect: it pulls behavior even without a body need: incentive theory

chain.cause: Arousal is too low or too high for the task
chain.effect: performance drops; it is best at a moderate level, lower for hard tasks (Yerkes-Dodson law)

chain.cause: An expected reward is given for something you already enjoy
chain.effect: your reason shifts to the reward and intrinsic motivation can fall (overjustification effect)

ideas: Instinct theory fits fixed, unlearned patterns in animals. Drive-reduction: needs create drives that push us toward homeostasis. Incentive theory: outside rewards pull us.
Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level of arousal. The Yerkes-Dodson law says performance peaks at moderate arousal, lower for hard tasks. Sensation seekers prefer high arousal.

Self-determination theory: needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness. Intrinsic motivation comes from the activity; extrinsic from rewards. Expected rewards can undermine intrinsic interest (overjustification).
Hunger: ghrelin (stomach) signals hunger, leptin (fat cells) signals stored energy, the hypothalamus integrates them; external cues also trigger eating. The need to belong is a basic motive.

misconception.wrong: Any reward will kill a person's interest in an activity.
misconception.right: The undermining effect is strongest for expected, tangible rewards given just for doing a task the person already enjoys. Surprise rewards and specific praise for good work usually do not lower interest, and rewards can help with tasks no one enjoys.

summary: Motivation theories explain different behavior: instincts for fixed animal patterns, drive-reduction for body needs and homeostasis, incentives for outside pulls, arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law for the best level of arousal, and self-determination theory for intrinsic motivation, which expected rewards can undermine (the overjustification effect). Motivational conflicts are approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance and multiple approach-avoidance. Hunger involves ghrelin, leptin, the hypothalamus and external cues; the need to belong drives social behavior.
